item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Katharina Fellnhofer, ETH Zurich

Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Thomas H. Allison, Texas Christian University

Pia Arenius, Emlyon Business School

Moren Lévesque, York University

J. Jeffrey Gish, Syracuse University

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (ETP) is committed to working alongside entrepreneurship scholars to advance transparency, replicability, credibility, and rigor in empirical research. This special issue encourages authors to preregister research plans, submit empirical studies as Registered Reports — papers that receive editorial decisions before empirical results are known — and engage with ETP's contemporary Registered Revision process. ETP is pleased to announce a virtual special issue featuring Registered Reports, supporting its longstanding dedication to methodological innovation.

A growing body of literature spanning multiple disciplines including entrepreneurship explores the importance of credibility and replicability in scientific inquiry and how scientific rigor can be improved. This call for papers reinforces these efforts in entrepreneurship research by specifically advocating for scholars to submit studies as Registered Reports. The Registered Report format has evolved rapidly from a niche innovation to a widely adopted practice. Since the introduction of the Registered Report format in 2013, more than 300 journals have embraced the approach.

The Registered Report approach is a powerful catalyst to enhance transparency, reduce publication bias, and increase methodological rigor — goals that are especially pertinent to entrepreneurship researchers navigating complex, interdisciplinary, and context-dependent phenomena. ETP established itself as an early leader in entrepreneurship research by publishing pioneering Registered Reports, through previous editorials promoting greater empirical transparency, and by offering Registered Revisions since the beginning of 2025.

The special issue welcomes high-quality interdisciplinary research that connects entrepreneurship with diverse fields. Research types suitable for the Registered Reports format include replication studies, new data collection studies, research on boundary conditions and mechanisms, theory elaboration, longitudinal designs, and field experiments, among others such as abductive research, qualitative research as well as exploratory quantitative inquiry and meta-science. Interdisciplinary co-authorship is welcome and encouraged.

Potential topics

  • Replication and Robustness in Entrepreneurship Research
  • New Ways to Collect Data for Entrepreneurship
  • Importance of Null Results
  • Boundary Conditions, Mechanisms, Mediators, and Contextual Sensitivity
  • Longitudinal and Panel-Based Studies (Using Secondary Data)
  • Field Experiments and Entrepreneurial Interventions
  • Theory-Driven Exploratory Studies and Qualitative Studies
  • Meta-Science and Methods in Entrepreneurship Research

Timeline

  • December 22, 2026: Deadline for Registered Report submissions

item.title: Advancing Management Research Through Theory Testing: A Special Issue of Replication and Reproducibility Studies
item.content:encoded:
William G. Obenauer, University of Maine

Robyn L. Brouer, University of South Alabama

Rachel Clapp-Smith, University of North Georgia

Ajay Rama Ponnapalli, Wayne State University

Andreas Schwab, Iowa State University

Jost Sieweke, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Chen Wang, Western Michigan University

Group & Organizational Management (GOM) has made an explicit commitment to publishing replication research and contributing to an ecosystem that supports replication research in the organizational sciences. By making this commitment, GOM joins journals such as Strategic Management Journal, The Leadership Quarterly, Entrepreneurship: Theory and Practice, and Journal of Management Scientific Reports in this endeavor.

As part of GOM's commitment to supporting replication research, this special issue aims to stimulate a continued stream of replication and reproducibility submissions to GOM well beyond the publication of this special issue. Focal studies (i.e., studies replicated or reproduced) are not required to have been published in GOM, but they should be of interest to GOM's audience.

The special issue welcomes three types of submissions. Registered reports require researchers to submit their introduction and methods description before collecting data and will include detailed descriptions for either literal replication, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication papers. Registered reports must include all methodological details as reviewers cannot grant acceptance in principle when methods lack transparency. Authors are encouraged to submit registered reports at least four months before the submission deadline to allow time for data collection. Importantly, authors must not collect data before their action editor gives acceptance in principle.

Literal replication or reproducibility study only submissions are limited to 2,000 words with limited introductions and discussion sections, with the majority of text focused on methodology and results. This recognizes the importance of bolstering the research record through literal replication and literal reproducibility studies.

Full-length submissions should use conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements. Authors are encouraged to include reproducibility studies and/or literal replications within their full-length submissions for benchmarking purposes. While conducting a literal replication before constructive replication is encouraged, it is not required, as conducting reproducibility studies or literal replications may sometimes be infeasible due to practical constraints such as limited access to samples.

Potential topics

  • Registered reports on literal replications, literal reproducibility studies, or multi-study replication designs
  • Literal replication and reproducibility studies (single-study submissions)
  • Full-length submissions using conceptual or constructive replication to advance knowledge through boundary testing or methodological improvements
  • Reproducibility studies and literal replications for benchmarking purposes within full-length submissions
  • Replication research advancing organizational sciences

Timeline

  • June 30, 2027: Initial Submissions Due

item.title: Registered Reports
item.content:encoded:
In cases in which results, whether present or not, may have important theoretical or practical implications, scholars are encouraged to submit a Registered Report. In this type of submission, authors submit the introduction, methods, measurement info, and analysis plan (but not the results) of a completed or planned study.

This abbreviated paper is then evaluated on the basis of the importance of the topic, the merit of the selected analytic approach, methodological rigor and quality, and potential for impacting down-the-road theorizing and/or practice/policy. As results are not included in the registered report, what was or is likely to be found has no bearing on the outcome of the evaluation. This is in line with the journal's willingness to publish papers reporting negligible or non-effects.

Potential topics

  • Empirical studies with important theoretical or practical implications
  • Research with rigorous methodological design
  • Studies reporting null or negligible effects
  • Organizational and management research

Timeline

  • January 1, 2025: Call for submissions opens
  • December 31, 2026: Submission deadline
